services.title: Twelve engineers, one deploy
services.concept: Modular monolith or services: team size, Conway's law, and when to split.
services.voice: Three teams, one main branch, and a merge queue with opinions.
services.briefing: Twelve engineers in three loose teams now share one codebase and one deploy. Orders run to a couple of thousand a day, and every Thursday someone's release waits on someone else's migration. The org chart has started drawing the architecture; the question is whether you hold the pencil.
services.dilemma: Do you draw harder lines inside the monolith, cut one piece out, or cut it into many?
services.disagreement: Experts disagree here. Fowler argues for starting with a monolith and splitting once the boundaries have proven themselves; Tilkov argues that a monolith rarely splits cleanly later, so you should design the pieces from the start. Both have case studies, and both say team size changes the answer.
services.readNext: Read Fowler's MonolithFirst and Tilkov's reply side by side, then the Team Topologies chapters on cognitive load and Conway's law. The disagreement is the lesson.

modular-monolith.title: Modular monolith: enforce boundaries inside mercadito-app
modular-monolith.optimizes: One deploy, one database, and boundaries you can still move cheaply.
modular-monolith.costs: A quarter of refactoring before it pays; rules that hold only as long as people keep them.

orders-service.title: Split orders into its own service, owned by one team
orders-service.optimizes: One team ships orders on its own schedule; the architecture follows the org chart on purpose.
orders-service.costs: A network call where a function call was, a queue to run, and a slower quarter while it is cut out.

microservices.title: Microservices: orders, catalog and notifications, all at once
microservices.optimizes: Every team its own deployable, eventually.
microservices.costs: Four systems for twelve people, the microservice premium paid up front, and a reliability dip while everyone learns.

events.key-engineer-leaves: Monday, 09:30. The engineer who knew why orders work the way they do hands in notice. Two weeks.

inspections.everything-ends-at-postgres: Site inspection: whatever the boxes say, every pipe on site still ends at the same Postgres. The boundary is drawn above ground only.

review.who-owns-what: Which team owns which part of the system after this decision, and does the drawing match the org chart?
review.what-it-costs: What got worse, and what did you give up to get the rest?
review.when-split: What would tell you it is time to split further, or to merge back?

rubric.grounded-context: The context names the constraints that actually shaped the choice (team size, traffic, runway, deploy pain).
rubric.names-ownership: The decision says who owns what: teams, boundaries, modules or services.
rubric.names-tradeoff: The consequences name at least one force that got worse, not only the ones that got better.
rubric.names-given-up: What was given up is written down in a full sentence.
rubric.revisit-trigger: The revisit trigger is a condition someone could notice, such as a team count or a deploy queue, not a hope.

services.mmBoundaryWork: Naming modules and enforcing their boundaries with a dependency checker takes about a third of a quarter from a team that would otherwise ship features.
services.mmFewerCollisions: Once orders code stops reaching into catalog tables, teams step on each other measurably less: fewer merge conflicts and fewer cross-team review requests within a quarter.
services.mmClearSeams: Explicit module boundaries remove some accidental coupling that nobody intended in the first place.
services.mmDiscipline: Module boundaries inside one codebase hold only while people respect them; every engineer has to know the rules, and review has to enforce them. At 80 engineers that is a full-time job.
services.mmOneDeploy: One deployable means one thing to monitor and roll back. With twelve people that is simpler; with eighty, one bad change from any team takes everything down with it.
services.mmBiggerBox: Running the monolith on bigger machines to absorb the load costs more each month, but less than operating new services.
services.mmReadableWithoutThem: When a key engineer leaves, the knowledge lives in one codebase that others already read daily. It still hurts, a little.
services.splitExtraction: Cutting orders out of the monolith, strangler-style, costs most of a quarter of the owning team's time before the new service carries real traffic.
services.splitTeamOwnsIt: A team that owns one service end to end deploys it independently and more often, which shows up in lead time within a quarter. The bigger the company, the bigger the gain.
services.splitNetwork: A network call, a queue and a contract replace what used to be a function call. Retries, timeouts and versioning arrive with it.
services.splitInfrastructure: A new service needs its own pipeline, environments, dashboards and on-call rotation, paid every month.
services.splitNewFailures: A new service adds new ways to fail: timeouts, a backed-up queue, a message handled twice. At larger scale, the same split isolates failures instead.
services.splitTwoSystems: Twelve people now carry two systems and the contract between them. At 80 engineers it runs the other way: each team carries one service instead of the whole monolith.
services.splitSharedDatabase: The service still writes to the shared Postgres. Two deployables changing one schema is coupling the boxes do not show.
services.splitContractWalksOut: When the engineer who designed the orders contract leaves, the contract stays and the reasons behind it do not. The new owners relearn it from incidents.
services.msBigBang: Splitting three services at once with twelve engineers stops most feature work for the quarter.
services.msAutonomy: Independent deploys raise delivery speed once teams are large and stable enough to own a service each; with three teams and four services, the gain is small.
services.msDistributed: Four deployables, a queue and a shared database: distributed tracing, contracts and partial failures become everyday work.
services.msPlatform: Each service needs a pipeline, environments, monitoring and on-call. Most of that platform is paid before it pays back.
services.msReliabilityDip: During the first quarter of running several services, incidents rise while teams learn which calls can fail and how.
services.msSystemsPerHead: Four systems across twelve people means every engineer carries more than one service in their head, plus the contracts between them.
services.msRunway: The extra infrastructure and the slowed delivery cost about a month of runway at Year 2 burn.
services.msOrphanedService: With more systems than teams, losing one key engineer leaves a service nobody fully understands. The next incident there takes longer to fix.
services.tacitKnowledgeLeaves: Losing a senior engineer with tacit knowledge of orders costs the team about a quarter of ramp-up for whoever inherits the work.
services.modularReservoirDry: Every order still lives in the shared database; boundaries in the code do not split the load on the data.
services.sharedDbCoupling: A separate service on a shared database is a distributed monolith: the outage is shared, and so is the investigation.
